explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. The song says "we give thanks, for Your Name is near." No long list and no fancy speech, just thanks because God is near. I wish my thank-yous were that clean, because mine usually wander off into a story about my mustache.

I get why you'd reach for that one, because thank-you songs often come after a big rescue. But this verse never mentions enemies running off. It says "we give thanks, for Your Name is near." The reason is right there in the line, and it's God being near.

explanations.answer: Because the harvest came in full
explanations.explanation: A full harvest would be a fine reason to say thanks, and I'd throw a party for it. But this verse doesn't mention a harvest at all. What it says is "we give thanks, for Your Name is near." The thanks goes to God because His Name is near.

Close, baker, but this one flips it around. The voice says "When I choose a time, I will judge fairly." So the one speaking is the one who chooses the time. Nobody else gets to set that timer, and I know about timers, because mine never listens to me either.
That's right, baker. The voice says "When I choose a time, I will judge fairly." The voice does the choosing, and it promises to judge fairly. The people don't pick the time.

Yes, that's the line. "When the earth and all its dwellers quake, it is I who bear up its pillars." Everything is shaking, and the voice is the one holding the pillars up. I once rattled one cookie sheet and panicked for an hour, so I respect this.

That sounds like a good picture, but this verse never mentions seas. The earth and its dwellers are the ones quaking. The voice says, "it is I who bear up its pillars." So it's pillars, and the water isn't in this line.

I can see why you'd go big with that one, but it isn't in this verse. When the earth and all its dwellers quake, the voice says, "it is I who bear up its pillars." The pillars are what get held up. No gates show up in this line.
That's it, baker. The voice says to the proud, "Do not boast." Boasting is when you talk yourself up. I've done it over a good batch, and my hat usually bonks something afterward.
Worry is a fair guess, since that's a word we hear a lot. But the voice isn't telling the proud to stop worrying. It says, "I say to the proud, 'Do not boast.'" The word you want is boast.
Wander has a nice ring to it, and I do it around my bakery all day. But that's not what the voice tells the proud. It says, "I say to the proud, 'Do not boast.'" So the word is boast.

Right, baker. The voice says, "Do not lift up your horn against heaven or speak with an outstretched neck." Think about that. Lifting your horn against heaven is aiming way too high. Even I know my limits, and my limit is the top shelf.

Neighbors make sense, because people do fight with the folks next door. But the voice doesn't mention them here. It says, "Do not lift up your horn against heaven or speak with an outstretched neck." The answer is heaven.

The temple is a good guess, but it isn't in this verse. The voice says, "Do not lift up your horn against heaven or speak with an outstretched neck." So heaven is what the wicked are told not to lift their horn against.

You got it, baker. After saying where it doesn't come from, the song says, "but it is God who judges." So the source isn't a direction on the map. It's God. That's one clear answer, and I love a clear answer.

An army looks like the obvious power on paper. But the song never names an army as the source. It says exaltation comes neither from east nor west, nor out of the desert, "but it is God who judges." The answer is God.

explanations.answer: From the kings of the earth
explanations.explanation: Kings are a natural guess, since they're the ones with the crowns. But the song doesn't point there. It says, "but it is God who judges; He brings down one and exalts another." So the source is God.

Yes, "down" goes in the first blank. The verse says, "He brings down one and exalts another." One gets brought down. I've been brought down by a cookie that stuck to the pan, but this is a much bigger deal.
That's right, baker. "Exalts" goes in the second blank. The verse says, "He brings down one and exalts another." Exalts just means lifts up.
Spares sounds gentle, and I see why you picked it. But the verse doesn't say that. It says, "He brings down one and exalts another." So the blanks are filled by down and exalts.
Scatters is a strong word, and I use it when I drop the sprinkles. But it's not in this verse. The song says, "He brings down one and exalts another." Down and exalts are the words that fit.

Back almost sounds right, like "brings back," which is a real phrase. But it isn't the phrase here. The verse says, "He brings down one and exalts another." Down fits the first blank, and exalts fits the second.
That's right, baker. The song says, "all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs." The cup is in the LORD's hand, and He pours from it. It's the wicked who drink it.

Priests are a natural guess, since they show up a lot in the Bible. But the song doesn't name them here. It says the cup is in the hand of the LORD, and "all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs." The word is wicked.

Kings are a fair guess, since they show up all over the Bible. But this verse isn't about them. It says, "He pours from His cup, and all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs." So the word is wicked.

Not quite, baker. The verse says the wicked "drink it down to the dregs." The dregs are the very last bits at the bottom of the cup. That's not a sip. I've never left a cookie half eaten in my life, and I'd never do it to a cup like this either.
Right, baker. The song says, "all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs." That means they drink all the way to the very bottom. It isn't a quick sip.

That's right, baker. After the cup, the song says, "But I will proclaim Him forever." The word that matters there is forever. That's a long time to keep talking, and I'm the guy who can't stop talking about one batch for ten minutes.
Hang on, because it actually does say it. After the cup, the song says, "But I will proclaim Him forever; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob." So the singer does say it. That makes this one True.

explanations.answer: Wicked horns cut off and righteous horns exalted
explanations.explanation: That's how it ends, baker. "All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted." The wicked horns get cut off, and the righteous horns get lifted up. It's a clear last line.

explanations.answer: Wicked horns exalted and righteous horns cut off
explanations.explanation: That one is flipped, baker. The song ends, "All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted." The wicked horns are the ones cut off. The righteous horns are the ones lifted up.

explanations.answer: Both kinds of horns cut off alike
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't treat both kinds of horns the same. It ends, "All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted." So the wicked horns are cut off. The righteous horns are exalted.
